title: The friend of Allah
hookLine: Ibrahim is called the friend of Allah for his wholehearted trust (4:125)
last: BUHITA — THE SUN RISES WHERE IT RISES.

lines: PEOPLE YOU KNOW, AND A FRIEND.
THE ONE YOU'D CALL FROM ANYWHERE.
cards: There are the people you know, and then there are one or two friends. Not the ones you follow, or work with. The one you could call from a hospital waiting room.
With that friend there's no performing. You can say the plain thing: I'm scared. I don't know what to do.
And they listen. Ibrahim has watched the stars, broken the idols, faced a crowd, a fire and a king. Kings have titles.
Prophets have titles too. But one name the Qur'an gives Ibrahim, the one Muslims still call him by, is the name for that kind of friend.

teach.b: Surah four, verse one twenty-five. In Pickthall's words: “Allah (Himself) chose Abraham for friend.” The Arabic word is khalil, stronger than the everyday word for a friend.
Some scholars trace it to the root kh-l-l, which has to do with the gaps between things, what passes through.

teach.h: KHULLA — A CLOSENESS ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
teach.b: Scholars explain khulla as a closeness that goes all the way through, a love that fills every space in the heart and leaves no room for anything else.
So when Ibrahim, watching the star set, said I love not things that set, he was clearing that space. Muslims still call him Khalilullah, the friend of God.

The city of Hebron, where tradition places his tomb, is called al-Khalil in Arabic to this day. Jews and Christians know him by the same title, friend of God, in their scriptures too. What does that friendship sound like?

In surah twenty-six, Ibrahim talks about God not like a subject to a king, but like someone describing the person closest to him. Paraphrasing: He created me, and He guides me. He feeds me and gives me to drink.

teach.h: WHEN I SICKEN, HE HEALS ME.
teach.b: Then, in Pickthall's words: “And when I sicken, then He healeth me.” Food, water, getting sick. The most ordinary parts of a day.
That's how a friend talks. And friendship goes both ways. Ibrahim trusted wholeheartedly: on the day of the fire, the report says, his words were simply: God is enough for us.
A khalil doesn't hold back half of himself. He says the plain thing, and he listens.

how: Muslims call Ibrahim Khalilullah, the friend of God, and many talk to God in their own words in du'a, the personal prayer that can be made any time, in any language.

o: a servant who obeys his master
a messenger sent to one people
a friend of the closest, truest kind

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: a friend of the closest kind

s: khalil is the everyday Arabic word for any friend
it names a closer friendship than the everyday word; scholars call that closeness khulla.
the city of Hebron is called al-Khalil in Arabic
after Ibrahim, whose tomb tradition places there.
Jews and Christians also call Abraham the friend of God
the title appears in their scriptures too.

games.q: you're Ibrahim, describing God to your people. how do you talk about Him?
o: through ordinary things: He feeds me, and when I'm sick He heals me.
games.why: he spoke of food, drink and sickness: "And when I sicken, then He healeth me." that's how a friend talks.

practice: If you pray, spend a minute talking to God like a friend, no formal words, just what today was like, what worries you, what you're glad of, the way Ibrahim talked about food and water and getting sick.
Then spend the rest of the time listening, in the quiet. If you don't pray, say those same plain things in your mind to the friend you could call from anywhere, and then listen.

wordCard.voice: Khalil. A friend of the closest kind, all the way through. The name God gives Ibrahim: Khalilullah, the friend of God.

orig.note: Arabic: a close friend, from kh-l-l; Ibrahim is Khalilullah, the friend of God (4:125).

carryVoice: Your line: a friend listens. It's the name Ibrahim still carries: Khalilullah. Day thirty-seven, done.
